items.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He later on – which I had nothing to do with – got with the [Count] Basie band and started getting popular with all those hits.

ctx.x: How did you begin to manage him? He called you?

I got to know Joe and followed up. We became friends. He later on – which I had nothing to do with – got with the [Count] Basie band and started getting popular with all those hits. Things happened with him. I’d see him when he came to town, hang out with him. We were close friends. When he decided to leave Basie’s band and go on his own, and things started happening, he called me up, and said, “Hey, man, take this telephone out of my ear.” That was our management agreement. “You take over this time, because I –…
Your agreement with him was with a handshake?

items.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: because the relationship was excellent with Basie

ctx.x: That’s great. When you first started working with Joe then, he had come out of that period where he’d had the hit with the Basie band. Was there a conscious decision with you guys at that point where you said okay, I did the big band thing, now I’m ready for a solo career, or did you find a group to play with him or was he kind of freelancing with different bands?

No, no, no, no, no. He went right into, went pretty much right into a group thing, you know. I think it was Junior Mance was one of the first pianists, and then later on he had several different pianists, I can’t recall exactly in what order and who was there. Joe probably told you that story. But it was a conscious effort to put together a group but it was like a small jazz group, because that was what was the popular thing at the time. So I remember Sweets Edison was in the group, and there’s a tenor player, I…
